title: Double-encryption key recovery

problem.name_latex: Double and multiple encryption key recovery
problem.name: Double and multiple encryption key recovery
problem.statement_latex: For independent $k$-bit keys $K_1,K_2$, given sufficiently many known pairs satisfying $C=E_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(P))$, recover the key pair. The ideal-cipher model provides a precise comparison for security amplification by repeated encryption. The ideal-cipher comparison counts encryption and decryption queries; explicit cipher implementations also use quantum gate and classical bit complexity.
problem.statement_text: For independent $k$-bit keys $K_1,K_2$, given sufficiently many known pairs satisfying $C=E_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(P))$, recover the key pair. The ideal-cipher model provides a precise comparison for security amplification by repeated encryption. The ideal-cipher comparison counts encryption and decryption queries; explicit cipher implementations also use quantum gate and classical bit complexity.

quantum.headline_latex: $\Theta(2^{2k/3})$ ideal-cipher queries, quantum meet-in-the-middle through claw finding.
quantum.headline_text: $\Theta(2^{2k/3})$ ideal-cipher queries, quantum meet-in-the-middle through claw finding.
quantum.details_latex: The forward and backward key domains each have size $N=2^k$, giving the optimal $\Theta(N^{2/3})$ query bound. Tuples of intermediate values from enough known pairs isolate the intended key pair. A quantum walk maintains subsets of forward and backward evaluations; its stored-value access and reversible cipher operations determine the full gate cost. The associated time-efficient construction uses $O(N^{2/3})$ memory.

classical.headline_latex: $\widetilde O(2^k)$ time and $O(2^k)$ storage, classical meet-in-the-middle.
classical.headline_text: $\widetilde O(2^k)$ time and $O(2^k)$ storage, classical meet-in-the-middle.
classical.details_latex: Matching forward encryptions against backward decryptions recovers the two keys; the ideal-cipher query scale is $\Theta(2^k)$. For a known explicit cipher, let $G$ be the gate count of the two-key verification circuit, including the supplied pairs. Its $2k$ witness bits give classical time $\operatorname{poly}(k+G)2^{O((k+G)/\sqrt{\log(k+G)})}$ by Boolean tensor contraction. Linear-size verification circuits have a subexponential classical bound in $k$.

strength.description_latex: Polynomial speedup of degree $3/2$ in the ideal-cipher meet-in-the-middle comparison, or an exponential-constant improvement from $k$ to $2k/3$. The mechanism is quantum claw finding.

hardware.description_latex:
The time-efficient algorithm requires exponentially large coherent lists and exponentially many reversible cipher evaluations. Logical workspace for a single encryption is polynomial in the cipher size, while coherent storage and circuit depth dominate a cryptographic-scale fault-tolerant attack.

{\small [Before ``ETH is false'', the explicit double-encryption comparison used classical $\widetilde O(2^k)$ meet-in-the-middle versus $\widetilde O(2^{2k/3})$ quantum claw finding.]\par}
